This course focuses on the specification, design, and analysis of software
development. This course includes propositional and predicate logic, sets,
and relations in how they relate to software development. Students will
examine the use of functions, recursive definition and induction, finite state
machines, formal languages, Turing machines, and the limits of computability
in the design of a software system. This course covers the following topics:
Catalog Description
• Logic: Convert logical statements from informal language to propositional
and predicate logic expressions; apply formal logic to model and analyze the
correctness of software constructions; inductively prove properties of
recursively defined functions.
• Discrete structures: Use sets, functions, and relations to model software
problems and solutions.
• Formal languages: Design a finite state machine to accept a specified
language; transform a non-deterministic machine to a deterministic one;
design a regular expression to represent a specified language; recognize and
use context-free grammar that represents a small expression language.
• Computability: Recognize incomputable problems that have no algorithmic
solution.
Course Materials

online)

○ Stein, Cliff L, Robert Drysdale and Kenneth Bogart. Discrete Mathematics for Computer
Scientists, Addison-Wesley, 2010.
○ Thomas H. Cormen and Charles E. Leiserson. Introduction to Algorithms, 4th Edition

G202
● This class is governed by the academic rules, which state: “Current and
prospective students at Onondaga Community College are expected to
adhere to the values of intellectual and academic honesty and integrity.
Violations of academic honesty will not be tolerated.ˮ Please refer to the
Academic Rules in the College Catalog to make sure you know your
rights and expectations as a student.
Cheating/Academic Dishonesty
● Any form of cheating will result in an automatic 0 for the assignment for
all parties involved. A second offense will result in an automatic F for the
course. Students are expected to complete their own assignments.
Copying or using data files or code from current or past students, or
from any other person or source (including online help services), will be
considered cheating. Students should read and familiarize themselves
with the BCC Academic Honesty policy
● Any student that stops actively participating in or attending class must
be administratively withdrawn from the class with a grade of X. An
administrative X grade has negative impacts on financial aid, veteransʼ
benefits, and athletic eligibility and can lead to the student being forced
to leave on-campus housing.
● After a student has missed 5 classes consecutively they will be
administratively withdrawn from CSC220.
Administrative X
Use of AI
Red Light: Generative AI Use Prohibited
The use of generative AI, technology that generates new content/outputs in response to a
user prompt or request, is not permitted in this course. While generative AI has capabilities, it
does not replace the unique value of human critical thinking and problem-solving skills. The
development of essential professional skills, such as the ability to produce original ideas,
generate hypotheses, and analyze concepts, is central to this course. To foster the
development of critical thinking and independent learning, all assignments must reflect the
student's original effort, including their original analysis, interpretation, and composition.
Presenting AI-generated content as one's own violates academic integrity. Refer to the
Academic Rules for policies related to Academic integrity.
Examples of what's not allowed:
Using AI to generate, create, or assist any part of assignments, quizzes,
and/or exams.
Using AI to complete problem sets or analyze data.
Using AI to summarize course readings.
Yellow Light: Generative AI Use Permitted in Limited and Specific Contexts
Generative AI, technology that generates new content/outputs in response to a user
prompt or request, can be used in this course, but only for specific tasks and with
instructor permission. For instance, generative AI might be permitted for brainstorming or
editing, but not for drafting entire papers according to assignment instructions and

chunks.content:
guidelines. Students are encouraged to ask questions about appropriate use. When
generative AI is permitted, students must be transparent and follow citation standards of
the course. Presenting AI-generated content as one's own violates academic integrity, and
all course work must reflect the student's original analysis, interpretation, and
composition. Refer to the Academic Rules for policies related to Academic integrity.
Students should verify the accuracy, potential bias, and overall reliability of generated
content and engage with course material and resources to ensure ethical and responsible
use of generative AI when allowed. Additionally, the librarians at Coulter Library are
available to help students learn how to assess information, including AI-generated content,
and assist with citations. Students remain responsible for ensuring the completeness of
their submitted work reflects their own intellectual contributions and understanding of
course learning outcomes.
Examples of what's not allowed:
● Generating full drafts of papers or other assignments.
● Using AI to solve math problems or conduct data analysis.
● Completing quizzes or exams with AI.
Examples of allowed use:
● Using AI to brainstorm initial research questions or explore different
perspectives on a topic.
● Assistance with grammar, style, and clarity of writing.
● Creating outlines or initial drafts (with substantial revision and
development).
Green Light: Generative AI Use Permitted and Encouraged
In this course, students are welcome to use generative AI, technology that generates new
content/outputs in response to a user prompt or request. Students will be taught how to
utilize GenAI responsibly and ethically to support learning and exploration of course
concepts. Students are expected to develop AI literacy, which includes understanding how
AI tools work, evaluating their output critically, and recognizing potential biases. To
prepare students for success in an increasingly AI-driven workforce, this course
emphasizes the use of AI tools responsibly and productively. When generative AI is used,
students must be transparent and follow citation standards of the course. Presenting
AI-generated content as one's own violates academic integrity. Refer to the Academic
Rules for policies related to Academic integrity. All assignments must reflect the student's
original analysis, interpretation, and composition. Students are responsible for verifying
the accuracy, potential bias, and reliability of generated content and for using generative
AI responsibly. Additionally, the librarians at Coulter Library are available to help students
learn how to assess information, including AI-generated content, and assist with citations.
Generative AI can support and enhance student engagement in this course.

How to write a professional email
● Body starts out with a greeting “Dear Prof.ˮ, “Good Morning/Afternoon
Dr.ˮ
● Followed by a comma
● Be quick and to the point. Context is sometimes necessary, but too much
will seem like oversharing
● End the email with an address of their time and thank them for their
consideration
Dear Prof. Cross,
My miniature horse service animal just had surgery and I have to pick them up
during class time.
I just want to schedule a time outside of your office hours to talk about the material
for this week. Thank you for your time and consideration of my request.
Best,
Bailey
